papers.title: Automated CTA-Based Assessment of Aortic Remodeling Through Volumetric Biomarkers in Type B Aortic Dissection
papers.abstract: Type B aortic dissection (TBAD) requires lifelong morphological monitoring using computed tomography angiography (CTA). TBAD separates blood flow into the true lumen (TL), the original aortic channel, and the false lumen (FL), created by the dissection. Although three-dimensional volumetric analysis may complement diameter-based surveillance, its clinical adoption is limited by the time required for manual segmentation, particularly in postoperative scans affected by metallic artifacts. This study developed and evaluated an automated CTA-based framework for volumetric surveillance of TBAD across native and post-TEVAR conditions. We propose AORTA-SCAN, a hierarchical multi-stage framework for automated segmentation of the aorta, TL, and FL, extended to stented anatomy through a metal-aware triple-input strategy. The system computes conventional diameter measurements and volumetric biomarkers, including the perfusion dissection index (PDI), defined as the ratio between perfused FL volume and total perfused aortic volume. Domain adaptation was achieved using transfer learning and partial-label learning across heterogeneous clinical annotations. In native cases, AORTA-SCAN achieved a global Dice score of 0.84 and significantly improved FL segmentation compared with the nnU-Net baseline (0.84 vs 0.71, p < 0.001). Volumetric analysis showed high agreement with expert references, with a mean PDI bias of -0.17%. In postoperative cases, TL segmentation remained robust (Dice = 0.90), while FL and stent Dice were 0.75 and 0.72, respectively. Processing was completed in less than 1 minute per case on a standard workstation. AORTA-SCAN enables automated volumetric surveillance of TBAD and supports scalable extraction of PDI and diameter biomarkers from native and post-TEVAR CTA.

papers.title: Equity gaps in the genetic diagnosis of monogenic cardiomyopathy: an intersectional analysis of race and gender in the All of Us Research Program
papers.abstract: Purpose: Diagnostic yield from genetic testing in cardiomyopathy depends on reference data and access to care, which differ by race and gender, yet are rarely studied jointly. Methods: We analyzed 414,830 genome-sequenced All of Us participants for predicted deleterious variants (PDVs) in 58 cardiomyopathy genes, comparing ClinVar classifications by race and modelling cardiac outcomes against matched controls and, within heterozygotes, by race and gender. Among GLA or TTR pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) carriers with cardiomyopathy, we explored Fabry disease or amyloidosis diagnosis codes by race, gender, income and education. Results: PDVs in White participants were more often P/LP (13.9% vs 12.0%, p<0.001), more so among heterozygotes with cardiomyopathy (29.6% vs 22.1%, p=0.004). Cardiomyopathy odds rose from missense to loss-of-function PDVs (OR 1.12-1.79). Twenty of 131 GLA/TTR P/LP carriers with cardiomyopathy had a syndromic code; White women had higher odds than non-White women (OR 6.50, 95% CI 1.35-31.34). Syndromic codes were nominally associated with higher income and education, and 47 of 48 carriers with income <$25k were non-White. Conclusion: Variant classification and syndromic diagnosis are less complete for non-White carriers, particularly women. Equitable precision cardiology requires more diverse reference data and analyses that treat race and gender as effect modifiers.

papers.title: Left ventricular systolic dysfunction in long-term aficamten therapy for obstructive HCM is rare, transient, and well-tolerated
papers.abstract: Aims: Aficamten, a novel cardiac myosin inhibitor recently approved in several regions for adults with symptomatic obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM), requires structured echocardiographic monitoring to assess for left ventricular (LV) systolic dysfunction (LVSD). We aimed to describe the incidence, severity, trajectory, and clinical correlates of LVSD during aficamten therapy in patients enrolled in FOREST-HCM. Methods: Serial echocardiographic examinations were performed to inform investigator-driven dose adjustments and safety monitoring. Patients were categorized by on-treatment LV ejection fraction (LVEF): any incidence of LVSD ( /=50%). A prespecified subgroup analysis evaluated patients with any LVEF >/=50% to /=50% in 10 (83.3%) patients after dose reduction and in one after transient interruption. One patient had persistent LVSD, having also experienced LVSD while receiving placebo in the parent study. Concurrent non-serious clinical heart failure occurred in two patients (0.5%; EAIR 0.3/100 patient-years), resolving in one, while the other (with prior LVSD on placebo) permanently discontinued aficamten. Additionally, 47 patients (11.5%; EAIR 8.8/100 patient-years) demonstrated LVEF >/=50% to /=50% to <55% appeared clinically benign, supporting structured echocardiographic monitoring and individualized dose optimization.

papers.title: A shared cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk marker phenotype: physiological context and prognosis
papers.abstract: Abnormalities in routine cardiovascular and cerebrovascular risk markers often cluster. We characterised their common pattern, the shared adverse physiological axis (SAPA), using systolic and diastolic blood pressure, low- and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol, triglycerides, glycated haemoglobin, body mass index and C-reactive protein. The pattern recurred across clinical cohorts and genetic data. The genetic direction retained an estimated 71.8-91.1% of the linear genetic information these eight markers carried for myocardial infarction and stroke. At similar total fat, participants with higher SAPA had more visceral and less leg fat. Differences in the variability and regional distribution of body fat contributed to weaker marker covariation at older ages, where anatomical associations persisted. The fixed clinical score also distinguished stroke prognosis among Chinese participants initially classified as low risk. Net stroke probabilities over approximately seven years were 2.560% (95% interval, 1.742-3.431%) and 9.351% (5.906-13.037%) in the low and high SAPA groups.

papers.title: External validation of the EK-LEF electrocardiogram model for left ventricular systolic dysfunction in three U.S. health systems
papers.abstract: Background: Heart failure is projected to affect more than 11 million U.S. adults by 2050, and reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) can be present before symptoms appear. Deep learning models can detect reduced LVEF from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG), but most have been tested only in the institutions that developed them, often after excluding patients with prior heart failure or recordings of poor quality. We evaluated EK-LEF, a self-supervised ECG model fine-tuned on low LVEF detection. Methods: A bidirectional Mamba encoder was pre-trained on 435,420 unlabeled MIMIC-IV ECGs and fine-tuned on 471,248 ECG-echocardiogram pairs from 235,969 patients at Mayo Clinic Rochester and the Mayo Clinic Health System. Mayo Clinic Florida served as the validation set and Mayo Clinic Arizona, a geographically distinct region, as the internal test set, each evaluated with one pair per patient. For external validation, Dandelion Health ran the model on one ECG from each of 17,500 patients at five hospitals in three U.S. health systems. The reference standard was LVEF [≤] 40% on transthoracic echocardiography within 15 days of the ECG. The primary outcomes were sensitivity and specificity. Results: In the Florida validation set of 14,880 patients, 9.9% of whom had LVEF [≤] 40%, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) was 0.951 (95% CI 0.947-0.955). In the Arizona internal test set of 16,298 patients (prevalence 9.2%), it was 0.955 (0.950-0.959), with a sensitivity of 85.0% (83.1-86.8) and a specificity of 91.7% (91.3-92.2). The signal-quality rule excluded 2.2% of internal test recordings and 0.9% of external ECGs. Among the 17,344 external patients, of whom 9.4% had LVEF [≤] 40%, the model reached an AUROC of 0.912 (0.906-0.919), a sensitivity of 85.7% (84.1-87.4) and a specificity of 81.8% (81.3-82.4), and its negative predictive value was 98.2% (98.0-98.5). Sensitivity ranged from 79.5% to 90.2% between hospitals, and specificity was lowest in patients with a recorded cardiomyopathy (56.1%). Conclusions: EK-LEF retained high sensitivity and specificity at hospitals outside the health system in which it was developed. A negative result may help identify patients who do not need echocardiography.

papers.title: Intravenous Inotropes and Mortality in Takotsubo Syndrome: A Nationwide Cohort Study from the SWEDEHEART Registry
papers.abstract: Background: Takotsubo syndrome, which predominantly affects women, is thought to be precipitated by catecholamine excess, yet unstable patients often receive intravenous inotropes. We examined the association between intravenous inotropes and 30-day mortality in a nationwide cohort. Methods: We identified all patients with a first angiographic diagnosis of Takotsubo syndrome in the Swedish Coronary Angiography and Angioplasty Registry from 2008 through August 2025, linked to coronary care and population registers. The primary analysis was a Cox model for 30-day death among patients with a coronary care record, adjusted for age, sex, diabetes, smoking, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and Killip class, with multiple imputation. Sensitivity analyses varied the covariates and standard errors and examined days 0 to 7 and 8 to 30 separately, and the association was estimated in women and men with an interaction term. Results: Of 3,458 patients (79.4% women), 141 (4.1%) received inotropes: 3.6% of women and 5.8% of men. Thirty-day mortality was 19.9% in treated and 1.7% in untreated patients. The unadjusted hazard ratio was 12.89 (95% CI, 8.20 to 20.26) and the adjusted hazard ratio 6.49 (3.49 to 12.08; P<0.001; E-value, 12.5). In sensitivity analyses, the hazard ratio ranged from 3.37 (1.88 to 6.03), with presenting symptom and laboratory values added, to 6.62 (3.63 to 12.08). The hazard ratio was 8.82 (4.47 to 17.39) for days 0 to 7 and 2.47 (0.65 to 9.36) for days 8 to 30, and 6.43 (3.15 to 13.16) in women and 6.59 (2.79 to 15.58) in men (P=0.96 for interaction). Conclusions: Intravenous inotropes were associated with higher 30-day mortality in Takotsubo syndrome, in both women and men, with most of the excess in the first week.

papers.title: Unresolved Cardiometabolic Care Gaps and Cardiovascular Outcomes: A Count-Stage Framework Across 3 Prospective Cohorts
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: People with the same number of unresolved cardiometabolic problems may be at different stages of care. Whether care stage provides information on subsequent cardiovascular risk beyond the number of unresolved problems remains unclear. METHODS: We analyzed longitudinal data from CHARLS, HRS, and ELSA. Measurements, diagnoses, and treatment information were used to classify care states at each landmark. Cohort-specific adjusted Cox models estimated associations with subsequent cardiovascular disease (CVD), heart disease, and stroke. We tested whether stage added information beyond gap count and whether count remained informative after stage was considered. We also directly compared blood pressure, glycemic, and lipid targets within the same stage. RESULTS: CHARLS included 7,899 participants. HRS and ELSA included 20,531 and 12,071 landmark observations from 12,933 and 6,491 participants, respectively. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs for CVD per additional gap were 1.31 (1.23-1.41), 1.18 (1.13-1.23), and 1.09 (1.03-1.16). With exactly 1 gap, HRs for treated but uncontrolled (TA) versus unrecognized (U) gaps were 2.09 (1.70-2.57), 1.34 (1.19-1.51), and 1.27 (1.07-1.50) after adjustment for the affected target. Single-gap care stage provided additional information on CVD and heart disease risk beyond gap count in all 3 cohorts. Outcomes also differed between 2 and 3 gaps after accounting for stage in CHARLS and HRS. Under cohort-specific definitions, TA was the most common glycemic gap stage in all 3 cohorts, whereas U predominated among lipid gaps in CHARLS and ELSA. CVD associations were stronger for unrecognized glycemic gaps than for unrecognized blood pressure or lipid gaps in CHARLS. At the TA stage in HRS, associations were stronger for blood pressure and glycemic gaps than for lipid gaps. CONCLUSIONS: Gap count and care stage provide complementary prognostic information. The count-stage framework first records how many cardiometabolic targets remain unresolved, then identifies each affected target and its care stage to describe where further assessment is needed. Key Words: cardiometabolic health; care cascade; care phenotype; management of multiple risk factors; cardiovascular disease; CHARLS; HRS; ELSA

papers.title: Genetically proxied NLRP3 activity and coronary artery disease risk: a drug-target Mendelian randomization study
papers.abstract: Background and Aims: Preclinical studies implicate NLRP3 inflammasome activation, which drives release of interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18, in vascular inflammation and atherosclerosis, and selective NLRP3 inhibitors are now in clinical development. However, whether lowering NLRP3 activity reduces coronary artery disease (CAD) risk in humans is unknown. We used human genetics to estimate this effect and its mediating pathways. Methods: A genetic NLRP3 activity score was derived by combining the effects of eight cis-NLRP3 variants on NLRP3 expression and three inflammatory biomarkers: C-reactive protein, glycoprotein acetylation, and neutrophil count. The score was validated against circulating interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18. Drug-target Mendelian randomization was used to estimate its association with CAD, cardiometabolic traits and other diseases studied in NLRP3 inhibitor trials. Mediation by cardiometabolic risk factors was quantified using the product-of-coefficients method. Results: A lower genetically proxied NLRP3 activity score was associated with lower circulating interleukin-1{beta} and interleukin-18, but with higher CAD risk (OR = 1.21, 95% CI 1.02 - 1.45, P = 0.032). It was also associated with higher systolic blood pressure, apolipoprotein B levels, and type 2 diabetes risk, which together mediated an estimated 87% of the association with CAD. The residual direct association with CAD was attenuated (OR = 1.03, 95% CI 0.85 - 1.24, P = 0.79). In contrast, a lower score was nominally associated with lower risk of gout, pericarditis, and Parkinson's disease. Conclusions: Lifelong lower genetically proxied NLRP3 activity was associated with higher CAD risk, largely mediated by adverse cardiometabolic effects, with no evidence of protection after accounting for them. These findings do not provide genetic support for lowering NLRP3 activity to reduce CAD risk.

papers.title: Automated echocardiography image quality assessment and its association with AI performance
papers.abstract: BackgroundEchocardiographic image quality influences clinical interpretation, yet its definition remains subjective and its impact on artificial intelligence (AI) systems has not been systematically evaluated. We developed EchoQuality, a deep-learning model for automated echocardiography quality assessment, and quantified the effect of image quality on AI performance across a broad range of tasks. MethodsA multidisciplinary co-creation process established a definition of echocardiographic image quality, which was used to annotate 6,474 videos for EchoQuality development and internal testing, and 1,000 videos for external testing. The impact of image quality on the performance of state-of-the-art AI models was subsequently assessed for the prediction of 12 measurements, and the detection of 5 moderate dysfunctions and 6 cardiac diseases across five international cohorts totalling 762,588 videos from 25,205 echocardiography studies. In addition, a quality-aware aggregation strategy was developed to mitigate the impact of low-quality images. ResultsEchoQuality achieved a performance comparable to the inter-observer agreement, while the agreement with an expert in a prospective, blinded best-clip selection experiment was 90.4%. In downstream AI uses, high-quality studies resulted in the highest performance in 97 of 122 (80%) of evaluations. The median performance gaps between high- and low-quality videos were 10% [5-20%] in the prediction of quantitative measurements (R2), 14% [7-20%] in the identification of moderate dysfunctions (sensitivity), 12% [3-20%] in the detection of diseases (sensitivity), 12% [9-15%] in view identification (accuracy), and 3% [2-5%] in left-ventricular segmentation (Dice score). Performance gaps were consistent across state-of-the-art models, datasets, and tasks. Finally, a quality-aware aggregation strategy improved performance in 88% (63 of 72) of the evaluations, with a median relative improvement of 5% [1-15%]. ConclusionsEchoQuality provides an automated assessment of echocardiographic image quality, a major determinant of AI performance. Incorporating quality-awareness may improve the robustness and clinical reliability of echocardiographic AI systems.

papers.title: The ACROSSS-study. The role of sleep characteristics before and after a cardiovascular event. Rationale and study design.
papers.abstract: Studies of myocardial infarction and stroke showed a diurnal variation with peaks in the morning and afternoon. So far, night sleep or napping have not been investigated as triggers for cardiovascular events via a case-crossover study. Therefore, the main question of the ACROSSS (Acute CoROnary Syndrome, Stroke and Sleep) study is how much the occurrence of a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack is associated with taking a nap shortly before (topic 1, case-crossover study, 656 patients needed). Moreover, the study aims at assessing the incidence of sleep disturbances three and twelve months after a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack (topic 2, follow-up study, 400 patients needed). Recruitment of patients is carried out in four German hospitals in Essen and Bottrop, North Rhine-Westphalia. The examination program includes the case-crossover questionnaire on potential acute triggers of cardiovascular events, a sleep questionnaire with validated instruments (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, etc.) and a questionnaire on health status and lifestyle habits. Moreover, eligible patients are screened for sleep apnea and during the follow-up sleep is measured by actigraphy. The combination of sleep-related and clinical data offers a deeper understanding of how sleep affects the acute onset of a cardiovascular event and recovery afterwards.

papers.title: Refining Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Risk Assessment Across the Heart Failure Spectrum
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) framework emphasizes risk assessment and prevention of heart failure (HF). However, the prognostic implications and optimal assessment of CKM burden in established HF remain uncertain. ObjectivesTo evaluate the prognostic value of binary and HF-adapted graded CKM burden scores across HF phenotypes. MethodsWe evaluated 2 independent HF cohorts comprising patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF) initiating angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor therapy (HFrEF- ARNI; n=1,450) and patients hospitalized for acute HF (AHF; n = 2,985). AHF patients were stratified by left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) into View larger version (39K): org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@19d0d20org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@1c8dfe3org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@e2ea71org.highwire.dtl.DTLVardef@18dbeeb_HPS_FORMAT_FIGEXP M_FIG C_FIG Binary and graded CKM burden scores were evaluated in the HFrEF-ARNI and AHF cohorts. The binary score captured the presence of six CKM components, whereas the graded score additionally incorporated reverse-scored BMI and CKD severity. The graded score demonstrated more consistent associations with the composite outcome of all-cause death or HF hospitalization, particularly in HFpEF. It also provided better prognostic performance across cohorts and HF phenotypes. Adjusted hazard ratios were estimated using multivariable Cox regression. Prognostic performance was assessed using Harrells C-index and likelihood-ratio {chi}{superscript 2}statistics. * P <0.05; ** P <0.01; *** P <0.001.

papers.title: Clinician gaze as a supervisory signal for electrocardiogram deep learning: a matched-control proof-of-concept study
papers.abstract: AimsTo assess what evidence is required to attribute an apparent effect of clinician-gaze supervision on an electrocardiogram (ECG) deep-learning model to gaze itself, separating target engagement, case specificity, and diagnostic preservation. Methods and resultsTen ECG stimuli interpreted by 63 readers yielded 12-lead gaze targets for nine consultants and 20 clinicians. A pretrained 23-output ECG network was fine-tuned with gaze-only loss on eight ECGs per cross-validation fold. Held-out gaze cosine improved modestly (consultants 0.858 to 0.872; all clinicians 0.884 to 0.898), but untrained training-fold mean gaze agreed better (0.929 and 0.951). Lead-occlusion concordance was weak (mean Spearman {rho} 0.236). On 2,198 PTB-XL fold-10 ECGs, macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) fell from 0.922 to 0.893 after gaze-only tuning; uniform and permuted controls also reduced performance. In a post hoc experiment combining PTB-XL diagnostic cross-entropy with gaze loss, macro AUROC was approximately 0.923 in diagnostic-only, real-gaze, uniform and permuted arms, but real-gaze targets were barely fitted even on training ECGs (cosine 0.858 to 0.860). ConclusionIn this sparse experiment, gaze-only optimisation engaged its target without demonstrating case-specific learning beyond a population viewing prior, and matched controls showed that the resulting diagnostic deterioration was not attributable to correctly matched gaze. Joint training preserved source-domain discrimination, but because gaze targets were barely fitted, whether gaze adds diagnostic value remains untested. Claims that human viewing has shaped a model require mean-gaze, matched-null and function-preserving controls.

papers.title: AortoBVI: A Machine Learning-derived Risk Stratification of Ascending Aortic Aneurysms Predictable by Imaging
papers.abstract: BackgroundCurrent diameter-based risk stratification for ascending aortic aneurysms incompletely captures patient-specific dissection risk. Here, we apply machine learning to ex vivo aortic biomechanics to define a tissue-derived risk continuum, termed aortic biomechanical vulnerability index (AortoBVI), and use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to predict this index in vivo. MethodsAscending aortic tissue from 353 aneurysms, 45 normal aortas, and 46 acute aortic dissections underwent biomechanical testing. Biomechanical features were used to train a classifier distinguishing normal-like, intermediate, and dissection-like biomechanical phenotypes. Magnetic resonance imaging was performed on 38 aneurysm patients pre-operatively and 8 normal controls. ResultsThe classifier achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.901 (95% CI 0.836-0.954). Among 38 aneurysms with pre-operative MRI, a model combining age, aortic stiffness index (ASI), and aortic pulse wave velocity (aPWV) estimated AortoBVI (R2 = 0.580), identifying dissection-like aneurysms with an AUC of 0.928 (95% CI 0.826-0.994. These results significantly outperform aortic diameter (R2 = 0.116, AUC 0.620). ConclusionThese findings demonstrate substantial biomechanical heterogeneity at similar aortic diameters and support biomechanics-based risk stratification of ascending aortic aneurysms. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIAortoBVI integrates five ex vivo biomechanical measurements into a continuous index anchored to normal and acute-dissection tissue phenotypes. C_LIO_LIAmong 353 ascending aortic aneurysms, tissue-derived AortoBVI revealed substantial biomechanical heterogeneity despite similar aortic diameters. C_LIO_LIA model combining age with MRI-derived aortic stiffness index and aortic pulse wave velocity estimated tissue-derived AortoBVI more accurately than maximum aortic diameter. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIAortic diameter alone does not fully capture the biomechanical variation among ascending aortic aneurysms. C_LIO_LIMRI-based AortoBVI could provide a non-invasive approach to biomechanical phenotyping that complements diameter-based assessment. C_LIO_LIBiomechanically phenotyping patients with ascending aortic aneurysms using AortoBVI may help individualize surveillance intensity and the timing of surgery. C_LI

papers.title: Real-World Cuff-Measured Blood Pressure Trajectories in 20,003 Consumer Wearable Users
papers.abstract: Consumer wearables increasingly allow users to log cuff-measured blood pressure (BP), but resulting BP trajectories are uncharacterized. In this retrospective cohort study, 20,003 adults with Elevated BP or Stage 1 or Stage 2 Hypertension logged BP via a consumer wearable platform. We modeled 6-month trajectories with linear mixed-effects models and examined associations of [≥]5 mmHg reduction with engagement and wearable-derived metrics. Adjusted systolic reductions ranged from -2.6 mmHg (95% CI -3.1 to -2.2) in Elevated BP to -12.1 mmHg (-12.5 to -11.7) in Stage 2 Hypertension; diastolic reductions were -3.7 and -9.2 mmHg in Stage 1 and Stage 2. Overall, 50.2% achieved a [≥]5 mmHg systolic reduction and 27.9% reached normal BP. App time, journaling, AI Coach use, and BP logging were associated with higher odds of reduction; longer sleep and greater physical activity accompanied lower BP. These associational findings support consumer wearables as potentially scalable BP-monitoring platforms.

papers.title: Kidney Function Variability and Cardiovascular Outcomes in Heart Failure: Effects of Empagliflozin in the EMPEROR-Reduced Trial
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlthough sodium-glucose cotransporter-2 (SGLT2) inhibitors improve cardiovascular and kidney outcomes in patients with heart failure (HF), the prognostic significance of intraindividual kidney function variability and its modification by SGLT2 inhibition remain unclear. We investigated these relationships in patients with HF with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF). MethodsThis secondary analysis included 3,492 patients from the EMPEROR-Reduced trial. A location-scale joint model (LSJM) simultaneously evaluated the associations of estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) levels, longitudinal slopes, and intraindividual variability from day 28 onward with the composite outcome of cardiovascular death or HF hospitalization. Patients were stratified into tertiles of estimated eGFR variability using common cutoffs across the empagliflozin and placebo groups, allowing comparisons of cardiovascular outcomes at comparable variability levels. ResultsGreater intraindividual eGFR variability was independently associated with increased cardiovascular risk (hazard ratio: 1.08 per 1 mL/min/1.73 m{superscript 2} increase in estimated standard deviation; P < 0.001). The model incorporating eGFR levels, slopes, and variability demonstrated the best fit. Empagliflozin significantly reduced eGFR variability compared with placebo (standard deviation ratio: 0.93; P = 0.005) and attenuated annual eGFR decline by 1.83 mL/min/1.73 m{superscript 2}/year, despite an initial eGFR reduction of approximately 2.5 mL/min/1.73 m{superscript 2}. Event-free survival progressively decreased with increasing eGFR variability in both treatment groups. Importantly, within each variability tertile defined by common cutoffs, empagliflozin-treated patients consistently exhibited higher event-free survival than placebo-treated patients. ConclusionIn patients with HFrEF, greater intraindividual eGFR variability was independently associated with adverse cardiovascular outcomes, beyond eGFR levels and slopes. Empagliflozin reduced kidney function variability and attenuated long-term eGFR decline, with more favorable cardiovascular outcomes observed even among patients with comparable levels of kidney function variability.

papers.title: Two Axes of Sleep, One Heart: Dissociating Objective Sleep-Disordered Breathing From Subjective Sleep Duration in Cardiac Risk
papers.abstract: BackgroundCardiovascular epidemiology has long treated "sleep" as a single exposure, although it denotes both an objective physiological state and a subjective behaviour. We tested whether these domains carry separable information about cardiac risk. Methods and ResultsWe derived an objective axis from 8,444 polysomnograms (Sleep Heart Health Study) and a subjective axis of self-reported duration from 407,303 adults in the 2020 and 2022 Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. Multivariable regression (n=213,489), quadratic dose- response modelling, sleep-stratified comorbidity networks, and era-stratified tests were combined. Objective sleep-disordered breathing was continuous and right-skewed (median apnea-hypopnea index, 31.8 events/h; median sleep efficiency, 69%) in a risk-enriched cohort. Both short ( 9 h) sleep were associated with disease after full adjustment: adjusted odds ratios for heart attack were 1.24 (95% CI, 1.19-1.30) and 1.30 (1.19-1.42), and for stroke 1.12 (1.06-1.17) and 1.42 (1.29-1.57). A positive quadratic term confirmed a U shape for all 4 outcomes formally tested (P[≤]6.3x10-{superscript 2}), with fitted nadirs of 7.26 to 7.85 hours. Suboptimal sleep also raised comorbidity-network density from 0.089 to 0.112 (short sleep; +26%) and 0.108 (long sleep; +22%), with non-overlapping bootstrap CIs and concordant effects across demographic strata. A survey-weighted replication in official CDC microdata (n=344,010; median design effect, 4.43) preserved the principal cardiac, U-shaped, and network findings; an exploratory COVID-19 interaction (P=0.020) did not survive design-based correction. ConclusionsObjective breathing pathology and subjective duration are separately prognostic, and suboptimal sleep amplifies the cardiometabolic comorbidity network. Duration alone cannot exclude asymptomatic sleep-disordered breathing; cardiovascular prevention should assess both axes. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat Is New?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn 8,444 full-night polysomnograms and 407,303 survey responses, objective sleep-disordered breathing and self-reported sleep duration behave as two separately measurable, non-interchangeable dimensions of sleep exposure. C_LIO_LISelf-reported sleep duration has a formally verified U-shaped relation with cardiometabolic disease, with fitted risk nadirs of 7.26 to 7.85 hours that fall inside the recommended 7-9 hour range. C_LIO_LISuboptimal sleep is associated with a 22-26% increase in cardiometabolic comorbidity-network density, a structural effect reproduced across every age, sex, and race/ethnicity stratum examined. C_LIO_LIA design-weighted replication in the official CDC microdata (n=344,010; median design effect, 4.43) preserved the principal cardiac, U-shaped, and network associations and identified the secondary findings that are sensitive to the survey design. C_LI What Are the Clinical Implications?O_LIA reassuring self-report of 7-9 hours of sleep does not exclude severe, asymptomatic sleep-disordered breathing, so patients with hypertension, atrial fibrillation, stroke, or resistant metabolic risk should be considered for objective sleep assessment irrespective of reported duration. C_LIO_LIA report of more than 9 hours of sleep warrants clinical attention as a marker of occult multimorbidity rather than being dismissed as healthy behaviour. C_LIO_LIThe Sleep Network Modulation Index offers a compact, reproducible summary of how a modifiable exposure couples multiple disease clusters simultaneously, and may be tracked in longitudinal cohorts or prevention programmes. papers.title: Shared genetic architecture between digestive infectious diseases and cardiovascular diseases: a genome-wide cross-trait analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundDigestive infectious diseases and cardiovascular diseases may share common genetic, inflammatory and immune-related mechanisms. However, the shared genetic architecture between these disease groups, the specific pleiotropic loci involved and the potential contribution of intestinal infectious diseases (IID) to cardiovascular risk remain incompletely understood. MethodsWe analysed publicly available genome-wide association study summary statistics for 36 binary traits of European ancestry, including 16 digestive infectious disease traits and 20 cardiovascular traits. Univariate linkage disequilibrium score regression was used to estimate SNP-based heritability and prioritise traits. Global and local genetic sharing were evaluated using cross-trait LDSC and SUPERGNOVA. Multi-trait analysis of GWAS, cross-trait sensitivity analyses, FM-summary fine-mapping and Bayesian colocalisation were used to identify and refine pleiotropic loci. Candidate genes and biological functions were investigated using MAGMA, tissue- and cell-type-specific enrichment analyses, transcriptome-wide association analysis and protein-wide association analysis. Bidirectional two-sample Mendelian randomisation and two-step mediation analyses using three independent gut microbiome GWAS resources were subsequently performed. ResultsSixteen traits passed heritability quality control, yielding 39 trait pairs with significant global genetic correlations after Bonferroni correction. MTAG identified 41 candidate SNP records and 14 trait-pair-specific lead-SNP records representing eight unique SNPs; 39 candidate records and 12 lead records involved IID. Fine-mapping and colocalisation prioritised eight records representing four unique variants. Locus-based gene prioritisation retained 24 candidate genes across four pairs. Gene-set enrichment identified 43 significant trait-pair-GO term associations, and tissue enrichment identified seven significant associations. Transcriptome-wide analyses implicated 21 candidate genes, and proteome-wide analyses identified four associations involving three proteins. After false discovery rate (FDR) correction, forward MR supported associations of IID liability with cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, atrial fibrillation and flutter, and ischaemic heart disease; reverse MR supported only cardiac arrhythmias to IID. Five positive exploratory microbiota-IID-cardiovascular mediation patterns were described. Only the Oxalobacter-IID-cardiac arrhythmias indirect effect reached unadjusted P < 0.05. ConclusionsDigestive infectious diseases, particularly IID, share substantial genetic architecture with cardiovascular diseases. Integrative genetic analyses identified recurrent pleiotropic loci, candidate genes and putative microbiome-mediated pathways linking IID with cardiovascular outcomes. These findings provide testable hypotheses for further functional validation and clinical investigation.

papers.title: Genetically Proxied NLRP3 Inflammasome Downregulation and Cardiovascular Disease
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe inhibition of NOD-, LRR- and pyrin domain-containing protein 3 (NLRP3) inflammasome is an emerging therapeutic strategy for atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD). Although early clinical trials demonstrate reductions in inflammatory biomarkers, whether these translate into cardiovascular benefit remains uncertain. We investigated the potential efficacy and safety of NLRP3 inhibition using human genetics. MethodsWe developed a cis-genetic instrument for NLRP3 downregulation using C-reactive protein (CRP) associated variants (P<5x10-) within the NLRP3 locus ({+/-}100 kb of NLRP3 transcription start site) from 575,531 participants. Mendelian Randomization and colocalization analyses assessed the effect of the genetic instrument against gene expression of NLRP3 and other inflammatory mediators in immune cells, downstream inflammatory biomarkers, and pharmacodynamic responses to the NLRP3 inhibitor ruvonoflast. Two-sample Mendelian randomization assessed cardiovascular, cardiometabolic, and infectious outcomes, followed by phenome-wide analyses of 1,387 clinical outcomes. ResultsUsing 14 variants in the NLRP3 locus, we constructed a genetic instrument that corresponded to a 19% difference in circulating CRP between the extreme percentiles of its distribution. Colocalisation evidence suggested the effects on CRP to be driven by reduced NLRP3 expression in naive monocytes (PP.H4=98.7%). In accordance with the expected biological role of NLRP3, genetically proxied NLRP3 downregulation by the constructed instrument was associated with lower IL-18 ({beta}=-0.11; 95%CI, -0.14 to -0.08) and IL-6 ({beta}=-0.15; 95%CI, -0.17 to -0.12) and broadly similar pharmacodynamic effects to the NLRP3 inhibitor ruvonoflast across 8 biomarkers. Genetically proxied NLRP3 inhibition was associated with lower risk of recurrent pericarditis (OR per 19% decrease in CRP, 0.68, 95%CI, 0.58-0.80), but slightly elevated risk of coronary artery disease (OR, 1.06; 95%CI, 1.03-1.08) and peripheral arterial disease (OR, 1.10; 95%CI, 1.04-1.15) and no effect on ischaemic stroke (OR, 0.98; 95%CI, 0.94-1.02). The instrument was also associated with higher carotid-intima-media thickness and a worse cardiometabolic profile with increasing effects on blood pressure, waist-to-hip ratio, LDL cholesterol, and triglycerides. We found no associations with increased risk for prespecified infectious disease outcomes. ConclusionsA genetic proxy for NLRP3 inflammasome downregulation reproduced key molecular effects of pharmacological NLRP3 inhibition but was not associated with reduced ASCVD risk. Clinical perspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat is new?C_ST_ABS- We developed a genetic proxy of NLRP3 inflammasome downregulation comprising 14 variants within the NLRP3 locus. - Mirroring the biology of NLRP3 signaling, genetically proxied NLRP3 downregulation was associated with lower IL-6 and IL-18 concentrations and showed broadly concordant biomarker effects with the oral NLRP3 inhibitor, ruvonoflast. - Despite mimicking pharmacologic NLRP3 inhibition at a biomarker level, genetically proxied NLRP3 downregulation was not associated with reduced lifetime cardiometabolic risk. What are the clinical implications?- In view of emerging therapeutic efforts to target NLRP3 inflammasome, we could not find human genetic evidence supporting that NLRP3 downregulation could reduce risk of cardiovascular events.

papers.title: An Interpretable DSP Architecture for ECG Rhythm and Premature Ventricular Contraction Detection in MATLAB/Simulink
papers.abstract: Electrocardiogram (ECG) monitoring requires reliable signal preprocessing and interpretable detection of abnormal cardiac activity while maintaining low algorithmic complexity. This study presents an integrated digital signal processing architecture developed in MATLAB/Simulink for ECG preprocessing, QRS and R-peak detection, heart-rate estimation, rhythm classification, and premature ventricular contraction (PVC) detection. Real ECG recordings from the MIT-BIH Arrhythmia Database were used for development and evaluation. The preprocessing stage employs minimum-order elliptic IIR high-pass and low-pass filtering, followed by differentiation, squaring, moving-window integration, thresholding, and R-peak detection. RR intervals derived from detected R peaks are used for instantaneous heart-rate calculation and classification of normal rhythm, bradycardia, and tachycardia. PVC detection uses two interpretable beat-level features, an RR-interval ratio and a QRS-energy ratio, combined through fixed rule-based logic. Three initial 10-s windows containing 18 annotated PVCs were used during algorithm development and threshold selection. After the detector parameters were frozen, evaluation was performed on nine additional non-overlapping 10-s windows containing 56 expert-annotated PVCs from MIT-BIH Records 106, 119, and 200. Using a {+/-}100 ms event-matching tolerance, the held-out evaluation produced 40 true positives, 9 false positives, and 16 false negatives, corresponding to 71.43% sensitivity, 81.63% precision, and 76.19% F1 score. Across the same nine windows, the R-peak detector achieved 94.39% sensitivity, 99.02% positive predictivity, 96.65% F1 score, and approximately 16.91 ms mean absolute timing error. The results demonstrate the feasibility and limitations of a lightweight and explainable streaming ECG-processing architecture and motivate future work incorporating adaptive decision thresholds and broader patient-independent validation.

papers.title: Early potassium response to mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist therapy and cardiovascular outcomes in primary aldosteronism: a landmark cohort study
papers.abstract: BackgroundMineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs) are standard therapy for primary aldosteronism (PA). Serum potassium is measured in nearly every treated patient, but the long-term prognostic value of potassium attained early after initiation is undefined. MethodsIn the TriNetX Research Network, we identified adults with PA newly initiating spironolactone or eplerenone in 2000-2025, without prior adrenalectomy (n=4,169; 180-day landmark design). Achieved potassium (last value on days 14-180) was categorised as <4.0, 4.0-<4.5, 4.5-<5.0 and [≥]5.0 mmol/L, and its change from baseline in tertiles, using cause-specific Cox and Fine-Gray models. The primary outcome was a composite of myocardial infarction, stroke or death; incident heart failure was co-primary. FindingsOver a median 3.0 years, 623 composite events occurred. Estimated risk was lowest at 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L (adjusted hazard ratio 0.65, 95% CI 0.52-0.83, versus <4.0 mmol/L), lower than the 4.0-<4.5 mmol/L band, and not different from [≥]5.0 mmol/L. A larger rise in potassium was associated with lower risk. A similar pattern was seen for incident heart failure (0.54, 0.36-0.80; 248 events). Potassium below the 3.6 mmol/L consensus threshold for hypokalaemia carried no significantly higher risk (1.22, 0.96-1.56). The change in potassium correlated weakly with the change in renin ({rho}=0.15). InterpretationIn MRA-treated PA, cardiovascular and heart-failure risk was lowest at an early achieved potassium of 4.5-<5.0 mmol/L, well above the 3.6 mmol/L accepted by consensus criteria as correction of hypokalaemia; correction alone may therefore be an insufficient treatment target. Whether titrating therapy towards this band improves outcomes requires prospective evaluation. FundingGrants from Taipei Veterans General Hospital (V114C-038) and the National Science and Technology Council, Taiwan (NSTC 113-2314-B-A49-040-MY3, 113-2314-B-A49-009, 113-2321-B-075A-002).

papers.title: Wavelet-derived indices of cardiac vagal and vasomotor oscillations as a new tool to better understand autonomic imbalance in post-COVID-19 dysautonomia
papers.abstract: BackgroundWhen aiming to quantify autonomic imbalance, conventional heart rate variability (HRV) analysis generally reduces each posture to a single spectral value derived from interbeat intervals (IBI) alone. This analysis based only in IBI obscures transient events during blood pressure changes. We propose two wavelet-derived indices that quantify cardiac vagal and vasomotor sympathetic oscillations separately and over time. Since autonomic imbalance is directly related to baroreflex sensitivity (BRS), we evaluated them against an estimate of baroreflex sensitivity in post-COVID-19 patients. MethodsIn this study, 121 participants (32 healthy controls and 89 patients with persistent post-COVID-19 autonomic symptoms) underwent an active standing test with continuous finger blood pressure. The continuous wavelet transform with generalized Morse wavelets yielded time-varying high-frequency power of IBI and low-frequency power of systolic blood pressure (SBP). Two new indices were proposed: Index I combined the magnitude and variability of HF IBI power (aimed to quantify parasympathetic activity), and the index J combined LF SBP power with the rate of its transient elevations (bursts), which aims to quantify sympathetic vasomotor activity; J/I was their ratio. Indices were computed for supine and orthostatic periods and compared with conventional HRV and BRS measurements. ResultsIndex I correlated strongly with HF power of IBI and was lower in all patient subgroups than in controls, Index J had only a weak relation with LF power of IBI. On standing, J increased most in the subgroups with the worst baroreflex function. Orthostatic J/I was higher than in controls amongst patients, while LF/HF showed no differences. J/I was inversely correlated with BRS, most strongly when standing, and more strongly than LF/HF also. Adding J to I raised the cross-validated variance explained in orthostatic BRS substantially. In one example patient, a window during symptoms showed vasomotor oscillations that were hidden in the posture average. ConclusionsWavelet-derived indices from routine beat-to-beat recordings separate cardiac vagal modulation from sympathetic vasomotor oscillations and their transients. J/I correlates with BRS impairment more closely than LF/HF, providing a potential alternative estimate of autonomic balance, and its time-resolved visual output allows analysis of clinically relevant windows within a posture. The new proposed variables allowed an evaluation of autonomic imbalance that could be applied to different pathologies.

papers.title: Cardiorespiratory Limits Exist in HFpEF Independent of Age and BMI
papers.abstract: BackgroundHeart-failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF) is a clinical syndrome marked by exercise intolerance associated with impairments in cardiac and respiratory performance. HFpEF is associated with age and weight; however, it remains unclear whether cardiorespiratory limitations exist independent of these comorbidities. HypothesisIndependent of age and BMI, there are cardiorespiratory limitations inherent to the HFpEF syndrome that have yet to be fully elicited. MethodsA patient cohort with a clinical diagnosis of HFpEF (HFpEF; N = 38) and counterparts without identifiable cardiopulmonary disease (control; N = 21) underwent phenotyping with echocardiography and cardiopulmonary exercise testing with invasive hemodynamic monitoring. ResultsStudy cohorts were similar in age, BMI and height (p=NS for all metrics). Body-surface area (BSA) (2.1 m2 v 1.9 m2, p < 0.05), atrial fibrillation prevalence (50 v 14%, p < 0.05), and average E/e (11.5 v 9.5, p < 0.05) were elevated within the HFpEF cohort. Peak VO2 (14.1 v 19.1 mL/Kg/min, p < 0.001) was also diminished among those with HFpEF. Resting (17.1 v 11.4mmHg, p < 0.001) and exercise wedge pressures (29.3 v 16.7mmHg, p < 0.001) were elevated whereas stroke volume (93.3 v 110.4 mL, p < 0.05) and cardiac output (Direct Fick; 8.0 v 9.8, p < 0.05) during exercise were diminished in HFpEF patients. FVC, FVC%, FEV1 and FEV1% were also significantly diminished in the HFpEF cohort. ConclusionsCardiorespiratory limitations exist as a feature of the HFpEF syndrome, independent of age and BMI. BSA remained associated with HFpEF in keeping with adiposity as a feature of pathophysiology.

papers.title: B-cell involvement supports anti-CD20 therapy in paediatric rheumatic heart disease: Proof of concept and initial safety
papers.abstract: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD) remains a major cause of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, yet no therapy targets its underlying autoimmune mechanisms.[1],[2] We combined transcriptomic analyses of rheumatic mitral valves tissues with a translational approach. Using a panel of 750 mRNAs, we found a marked upregulation of B-cell-related pathways, including CD20-associated and multiple immunoglobulin genes, supporting a pathogenic role of B cells in RHD. We therefore evaluated an anti-CD20 B-cell depleting monoclonal antibody (Rituximab), in a feasibility study in children with RHD, in Dakar, Senegal. Treatment was well tolerated, and in the following RCT first year preliminary safety analysis asked by the ethical committee, children who received rituximab showed a decrease in anti-streptolysin O titers and clinical improvement compared to controls. This proof-of-concept reveals B cells as a therapeutic target and suggests that an anti-CD20 agent may represent a potential disease-modifying therapy for RHD.

papers.title: Reconstructing the range-normalized terminal QRS from V1 and V6 using the time-embedded 3D ECG
papers.abstract: ObjectiveCan a fixed V1/V6 projection of the time-embedded 3D ECG estimate the final 40 ms of V2-V5 more accurately than a fitted single lead? MethodsWe used simultaneous recordings from the Lobachevsky University Electrocardiography Database (LUDB), with cardiologist-annotated QRS complexes in all six chest leads. We fitted both models in 118 patients and tested them in 80 others. Root mean squared error (RMSE) is expressed in percentage points (pp) of the target leads 10-second amplitude range. ResultsIn 733 test beats, patient-weighted terminal RMSE fell from 12.58 to 10.64 pp (difference 1.94 pp, 95% bootstrap confidence interval 1.30 to 2.55). Reductions were 3.23, 2.85 and 1.35 pp in V3, V4 and V5. In V2 the difference was 0.35 pp (95% interval - 0.35 to 1.05). In 702 matched beats from 77 patients, the overall advantage was 2.22 pp at the automatic V1/V6 end and 1.92 pp at the annotated target end. Of 1,498 beat-lead pairs with whole-QRS correlation[≥] 0.95, 28.84% still had terminal RMSE of at least 10 pp. ConclusionsA fixed V1/V6 projection improved offline estimates of relative terminal amplitude in V3-V5 without fitting the target lead in the new patient. The gain was largest in V3 and V4 and uncertain in V2. Whether a reconstructed trace preserves a clinically recognizable notch or slur remains untested.

papers.title: Distinct circulating proteomic patterns associated with thoracic aortic diameter and stiffness: A proteome-wide study in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: BackgroundThoracic aortic aneurysm (TAA) is characterized by abnormal dilation and functional remodelling of the thoracic aorta. Current detection and surveillance rely largely on imaging, limiting population-wide risk stratification. Circulating proteins may provide biological insight into aortic remodelling and support future biomarker development. We aimed to identify circulating proteomic patterns associated with imaging-derived thoracic aortic diameter and aortic stiffness in a large population-based cohort. MethodsA proteome-wide association study was conducted in 6773 UK Biobank participants with available plasma proteomic and cardiac imaging data. A combined thoracic aortic diameter was derived from taking the maximum of standardized ascending and descending measurements, while stiffness was derived using a pressure-free index of aortic wall properties. Associations with 2920 circulating proteins were evaluated using multivariable linear regression with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Functional enrichment analysis was performed using the complete ranked protein list across Hallmark, curated, and Gene Ontology Biological Process collections. Principal component analysis (PCA) was performed as a secondary analysis to explore shared and divergent variation between the two phenotypes. ResultsIn age- and sex-adjusted analyses, 358 proteins were associated with aortic diameter and 60 with stiffness after FDR correction. Sequential adjustment materially altered these associations; in the primary fully adjusted models, 417 proteins were associated with diameter and six with stiffness. Functional enrichment analyses highlighted complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix organization, and contractile pathways associated with aortic diameter. In contrast, although only a few individual proteins were associated with stiffness, rank-based pathway analysis across the full proteome identified a distinct enrichment pattern involving cytokine signalling, protein processing, and intracellular transport. Aortic diameter and stiffness were only modestly correlated (r = 0.21). Secondary PCA showed that the first principal component (PC1) largely overlapped with the diameter-associated profile, with 310 of 370 PC1-associated proteins also associated with diameter. Four proteins (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) were associated with both diameter and stiffness in addition to being associated with PC1. ConclusionCirculating proteomic profiling identified markedly different and minimally overlapping molecular patterns associated with thoracic aortic diameter and stiffness. Structural dilation was primarily linked to complement/coagulation, extracellular matrix, and contractile pathways, whereas stiffness reflected a smaller, more distinct aspect of aortic remodelling involving cytokine signalling and cellular transport processes. The four shared proteins across both phenotypes (REN, BCAN, GGH and THY1) represent candidates for further biomarker and causal investigation.

papers.title: Sleep Irregularity and Risk of Incident Hypertension in the UK Biobank
papers.abstract: BackgroundIrregular sleep patterns are common and have been associated with higher cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk. Hypertension is the leading modifiable cause of CVD, but evidence linking irregular sleep to hypertension is inconsistent. The objective of this study was to quantify associations between irregular sleep and incident hypertension. MethodsWe conducted a prospective cohort study among 55,572 UK Biobank participants without hypertension or anti-hypertensive medication use who provided [≥]5 valid days of accelerometry in 2013- 2015 (60% women, mean age 61 years). We measured sleep regularity using the intra-individual standard deviation (SD) of sleep duration and the sleep regularity index (SRI), a measure of the similarity of sleep-wake patterns from one day to the next. Cox proportional hazards models estimated adjusted hazard ratios (HR) for incident hypertension, identified through linked health records, by levels of sleep regularity adjusting for demographic, socioeconomic, and lifestyle factors as well as employment schedule. We also evaluated differences by demographic, clinical, and sleep-related (defined by duration, efficiency, timing, and sleep disorders) subgroups, and interaction with genetic susceptibility to hypertension. ResultsDuring 7.9 years of follow-up, 5,713 participants developed hypertension. Participants with sleep duration SD >90 minutes had an 18% higher risk of incident hypertension compared to those with sleep duration SD [≤]30 minutes (HR: 1.18; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.06, 1.31). Similarly, participants in the lowest SRI quintile had a 40% higher risk than those in the highest SRI quintile (HR: 1.40; 95% CI: 1.29, 1.52). These associations were generally consistent across demographic, health, and sleep-defined subgroups. Sleep irregularity and genetic susceptibility contributed independently to hypertension risk, without evidence of interaction. ConclusionsIrregular sleep patterns were associated with higher incident hypertension risk independent of established risk factors and genetic susceptibility. Maintaining regular sleep schedules may represent a modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention. Clinical PerspectiveO_ST_ABSWhat is new?C_ST_ABSO_LIIn this large prospective study using objectively measured sleep from wrist accelerometry, greater overall variability in sleep duration and more irregular day-to-day sleep-wake patterns were independently associated with higher risk of incident hypertension. C_LIO_LIAssociations were robust to adjustment for potential confounding by demographic, socioeconomic, clinical, and lifestyle factors and were generally consistent across demographic, clinical, and sleep-defined subgroups. C_LIO_LISleep regularity and genetic susceptibility to hypertension were independently associated with hypertension risk, with no evidence that inherited risk modified the association between irregular sleep and incident hypertension. C_LI What are the clinical implications?O_LIMaintaining consistent sleep schedules may represent an important modifiable behavioral target for hypertension prevention alongside established lifestyle recommendations. C_LIO_LIThe association between irregular sleep and hypertension was observed regardless of genetic susceptibility, suggesting that improving sleep regularity may benefit individuals across the spectrum of inherited hypertension risk. C_LIO_LIThese findings support future randomized clinical trials to determine whether interventions that improve sleep regularity can reduce blood pressure and prevent hypertension. C_LI

papers.title: Feasibility of AI-Guided Handheld Echocardiography for Rheumatic Heart Disease Screening by Non-Cardiologists in Rural Nepal: A Mixed-Methods Diagnostic Accuracy Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundRheumatic heart disease remains a major cause of preventable morbidity and mortality in rural Nepal, where access to cardiovascular specialists and echocardiography is limited. We evaluated the diagnostic accuracy and feasibility of AI-guided echocardiography performed by nurse practitioners for community-based RHD screening. MethodsWe conducted a triangulation mixed-methods study (QUAN > qual) combining a paired cross-sectional diagnostic accuracy study with semi-structured interviews during community screening camps in Damak, Nepal, in November 2025. Nurse practitioners performed AI-guided handheld echocardiography using EchoNous Kosmos Plus devices, with cardiologist overread serving as the comparator. Diagnostic performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and kappa. Interviews were analyzed thematically. ResultsOf 90 participants enrolled, 76 were included in the final analysis. Mean age was 50.8 years, 57.8% were male, and 42.2% had undergone prior cardiac evaluation. Detection of any valvular lesion demonstrated 95.8% sensitivity and 100% specificity, with near-perfect agreement with cardiologist interpretation ({kappa}=0.97). Lesion-specific performance included mitral regurgitation sensitivity 66.7% and specificity 97.3% ({kappa}=0.55), mitral stenosis sensitivity 100% and specificity 97.2% ({kappa}=0.81), aortic regurgitation sensitivity 90.9% and specificity 96.9% ({kappa}=0.84), and tricuspid regurgitation sensitivity and specificity of 100% ({kappa}=1.00). Mean scan duration was 5.8 minutes. Portability, AI-assisted acquisition, and remote review facilitated implementation, while training needs, workflow constraints, and technical issues were barriers. ConclusionsAI-guided handheld echocardiography performed by nurses demonstrated high diagnostic accuracy and feasibility for rural RHD screening. AI-assisted task-shifting may expand access to early RHD detection in underserved settings.

papers.title: Mental Stress-Induced Peripheral Microvascular Dysfunction and Cardiovascular Events after a Premature Myocardial Infarction: A Prospective Cohort Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundImpaired macrovascular function during acute mental stress predicts adverse events in coronary artery disease, but microvascular stress responses are less understood. Because psychosocial stress and coronary microvascular dysfunction are more common in women, sex differences also warrant study. MethodsWe studied individuals aged 18-60 years within 8 months of a myocardial infarction (MI) who underwent a standardized mental stress challenge and were followed for cardiovascular events. We measured peripheral microvascular function with the reactive hyperemia index (RHI) before and after stress; abnormal RHI was defined as [≤]1.67. We also measured brachial flow-mediated vasodilation (FMD), interleukin-6 (IL-6), and myocardial ischemia. The primary endpoint was a composite of cardiovascular death, nonfatal MI, stroke, or heart failure hospitalization; a secondary endpoint included recurrent events. Cox regression examined stress-induced RHI decline, adjusting for pre-stress RHI and demographic, clinical, and psychological factors. ResultsAmong 487 participants (mean age 51 years; 43% women), 89 first and 90 recurrent events occurred over a median 34 months. Women had lower RHI than men before and after stress, and a larger stress-induced decline. Each standard deviation stress-induced RHI decline was associated with 36% higher risk of first events (hazard ratio [HR], 1.36, 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01, 1.82) and 44% higher risk of cumulative events (HR, 1.44, 95% CI, 1.04, 2.00), with no significant sex interaction. Abnormal post-stress RHI conferred adjusted HRs of 2.59 (95% CI, 1.13, 5.92) in women and 2.09 (95% CI, 1.11, 3.93) in men; abnormal pre-stress RHI was not predictive (HR, 1.12, 95% CI, 0.71, 1.76). IL-6 and FMD changes and stress-induced ischemia were related to RHI decline but did not explain its association with outcome. ConclusionsMicrovascular dysfunction with mental stress is more prevalent in women, and signals an elevated cardiovascular risk after MI in both women and men. What is already known on this topicMacrovascular dysfunction in response to acute mental stress has been related to increased risk of recurrent events in people with coronary artery disease. However, less is known about microvascular responses to stress. What this study addsA decline in microvascular function with mental stress is an independent predictor of subsequent cardiovascular events after a myocardial infarction (MI), and a stronger predictor than pre-stress microvascular function alone. Women have worse resting microvascular function and a more adverse microvascular response to stress. How this study might affect research, practice or policyMicrovascular dysfunction may represent an important pathway linking psychological stress to adverse cardiovascular outcomes in people with MI. The microvascular response to stress should be evaluated as a potentially modifiable marker of cardiovascular risk and intervention studies should determine whether targeting stress-related microvascular dysfunction can reduce cardiovascular risk in this population.

papers.title: Oxygen Uptake Efficiency Slope (OUES) and Mortality in Chronic Heart Failure: Comparisons of Absolute and Percent-predicted Values across Different Equations
papers.abstract: AimThe oxygen uptake efficiency slope (OUES) is a prognostic indicator obtained from cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPX) in chronic heart failure (CHF) patients. Although various equations exist for calculating predicted OUES, it remains unclear whether absolute or percent-predicted values offer a more accurate prognostic assessment. To investigate and compare mortality prediction in CHF patients using the OUES absolute values or the percent-predicted approach, incorporating the equations of Hollenberg, Buys, and Milani. MethodsRetrospective cohort study involving CHF patients evaluated at a tertiary university hospital between July 2013 and July 2023. All patients underwent maximal CPX and were followed in a specialized outpatient clinic. The primary outcome was all-cause mortality. To compare the prognostic accuracy between different approaches, we performed receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis and Cox proportional hazards regression. ResultsA total of 1.180 patients were included, 57% male, with a mean age of 55 {+/-} 12 years. The median follow-up was 5.0 years (IQR 3.0 to 7.2 years), resulting in 147 deaths (12.5%). The area under de curve (AUC) was 0.71 to 0.72 for males, and 0.60 to 0.63 for females, without statistical difference in the AUC between absolute and percent-predicted OUES. Different cut-offs were identified for each sex for predicting mortality and all OUES metrics remained independent predictors in multivariate models using sex and age. ConclusionsOUES, in both absolute and percent-predicted forms, demonstrated similar accuracy in predicting mortality in CHF, with sex-specific cut-offs influencing clinical assessment. Condensed AbstractO_ST_ABSAimC_ST_ABSCompare absolute and percent-predicted OUES (Hollenberg, Buys, Milani) for mortality prediction in chronic heart failure. MethodsRetrospective cohort of 1,180 patients undergoing maximal CPX. ResultsBoth approaches showed similar prognostic accuracy, with sex-specific cut-offs. ConclusionsAbsolute and predicted OUES independently predicted mortality, supporting either approach for clinical risk stratification. Main PerspectiveCardiopulmonary exercise testing plays a central role in risk stratification for patients with heart failure, and the oxygen uptake efficiency slope (OUES) is a robust prognostic marker even when maximal effort is not achieved. In this study of more than 1,100 patients, absolute and age- and sex-adjusted OUES showed comparable accuracy for predicting mortality. We also identified sex-specific OUES thresholds, supporting a more individualized approach to prognostic assessment and clinical decision-making in heart failure.

papers.title: VectBox Sync: a web application for vectorcardiographic analysis of ventricular synchrony from 12-lead electrocardiograms
papers.abstract: We introduce VectBox Sync, a browser-based application that implements a published vectorcardiographic (VCG) dyssynchrony index for exploratory assessment of ventricular electrical synchrony from the 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG). Despite guideline-directed patient selection, a substantial fraction of patients who receive cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) do not obtain the expected benefit. QRS duration and morphology remain the principal electrical criteria, yet they do not capture the three-dimensional trajectory of ventricular activation. VectBox Sync prioritizes native digital ECG recordings, including matrices and common clinical and research waveform formats; optional manufacturer-PDF import and externally digitized numerical files extend access when paper-like archives are the only available source. After optional preprocessing, the user selects a QRS interval, and the application calculates the dyssynchrony index relative to a calibrated control cutoff. It also provides companion VCG descriptors (voltage and speed integrals, loop angles, and planarity), together with VCG trajectories, synchrony-field maps, and a multilingual PDF report. Labeled conditions from the same session can be overlaid for comparison, for example across successive pacing settings. VectBox Sync makes this VCG-based assessment accessible through an integrated web application, providing quantitative descriptors that complement conventional ECG criteria. The application is available at https://vectbox.com/sync for research and educational use.
